buildSteps.title: Pick quiet sites spread in longitude
buildSteps.detail: Radio observatories need protection from interference, and stations roughly a third of the world apart in longitude let at least one dish see a distant spacecraft as the Earth turns.

buildSteps.title: Build the dish and its mount
buildSteps.detail: A reinforced concrete and steel pedestal carries a steerable mount that tracks a target moving against the stars at arcsecond precision.

buildSteps.title: Fit the precision reflector
buildSteps.detail: Reflector panels are aligned so the dish surface departs from a perfect parabola by a small fraction of the shortest wavelength used; beam-waveguide optics route the signal to equipment rooms below.

buildSteps.title: Install the receive chain
buildSteps.detail: Cryogenically cooled amplifiers are mounted as close to the feed as possible so that added noise stays below the noise of the sky itself.

buildSteps.title: Install the transmitters
buildSteps.detail: High-power amplifiers feed uplink signals into the same dish through a diplexer, giving enough power at the spacecraft for command and ranging.

buildSteps.title: Wire in the clocks and back end
buildSteps.detail: Hydrogen masers distribute a single reference frequency, and demodulators, decoders and command generators turn carriers into data and back.

buildSteps.title: Add optical ground terminals
buildSteps.detail: Telescopes with adaptive optics and photon-counting detectors are built to catch a laser beam that may arrive as only a few photons per bit.

buildSteps.title: Deploy relay orbiters
buildSteps.detail: Relay spacecraft are inserted around a planet or the Moon and linked to both the surface assets and the ground network.

buildSteps.title: Integrate and schedule the network
buildSteps.detail: Stations, spacecraft teams and relay passes are coordinated so that coverage is handed from one longitude to the next without gaps.
